title: About
text:
Olamide Akeboi
I am a public health researcher and spatial analyst based in Nigeria, with expertise in spatial modelling, Bayesian geospatial methods, monitoring and evaluation, and AI applications in global health.
I created Data for Impact to make rigorous analytical methods accessible to the people doing the hardest work in public health: the analysts, researchers, and programme teams whose findings should be driving decisions but often aren’t.
Every tutorial in this series is built around real problems, uses publicly available African health datasets, and includes full R code you can run immediately.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
You have spent days cleaning data, running analysis, and building a chart. You present it. The room nods. Nothing changes.
This is not a data problem. It is a communication problem — and it starts with your chart title.
This tutorial walks through exactly why most public health charts fail to drive decisions, and how to fix them using Nigerian immunisation data from the 2023–24 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and R.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
You have spent days cleaning data, running analysis, and building a chart. You present it. The room nods. Nothing changes.
This is not a data problem. It is a communication problem — and it starts with your chart title.
This tutorial walks through exactly why most public health charts fail to drive decisions, and how to fix them using Nigerian immunisation data from the 2023–24 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and R.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
What you will learn
By the end of this tutorial you will be able to:

Explain why chart titles are the most powerful design decision in any policy visual
Reframe descriptive chart labels into decision-driving arguments
Build a clean, policy-ready bar chart in R using ggplot2
Use ggtext to add formatted titles that direct attention
Use patchwork to create before-and-after chart comparisons

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Prerequisites
Before starting, make sure you have:

R and RStudio installed on your computer
A basic understanding of R — you can open a script and run code
The following packages installed — if you do not have them, run this in your RStudio Console:


install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggtext", "patchwork", "scales", "dplyr"))

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
The data
We will use state-level Penta3 coverage estimates from the 2023–24 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) — specifically the percentage of children aged 12–23 months who received three doses of the pentavalent vaccine, by state.
The full report is publicly available at dhsprogram.com.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 1 — Load your packages
Every R session starts by loading the packages you need. Think of packages as toolboxes, each one gives you a specific set of tools.

# Load packages
library(ggplot2)   # for building charts
library(ggtext)    # for formatted text in chart titles
library(patchwork) # for combining multiple charts
library(scales)    # for formatting axis labels as percentages
library(dplyr)     # for organising and transforming data

Each library() call tells R: “I want to use the tools in this package today.”

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 2 — Enter the data
We create our dataset using data.frame() — R’s way of building a table directly in your script.
The coverage values below come from Table 15 of the 2023–24 Nigeria DHS Key Indicators Report. Enter them exactly as shown:

# Create the dataset
coverage <- data.frame(
  state = c(
    "Abia", "Adamawa", "Akwa Ibom", "Anambra", "Bauchi",
    "Bayelsa", "Benue", "Borno", "Cross River", "Delta",
    "Ebonyi", "Edo", "Ekiti", "Enugu", "FCT",
    "Gombe", "Imo", "Jigawa", "Kaduna", "Kano",
    "Katsina", "Kebbi", "Kogi", "Kwara", "Lagos",
    "Nasarawa", "Niger", "Ogun", "Ondo", "Osun",
    "Oyo", "Plateau", "Rivers", "Sokoto", "Taraba",
    "Yobe", "Zamfara"
  ),
  penta3_coverage = c(
    79.7, 59.2, 72.8, 78.6, 58.2,
    73.4, 44.3, 42.2, 94.6, 85.7,
    75.9, 84.5, 75.9, 81.6, 84.8,
    59.8, 83.4, 62.2, 48.0, 47.5,
    53.3, 13.1, 37.1, 34.9, 87.6,
    67.1, 36.7, 73.9, 63.9, 67.1,
    52.6, 47.1, 71.0, 10.9, 47.3,
    51.3, 12.6
  )
)







Note



Penta3 coverage figures are from Table 15 of the 2023–24 Nigeria DHS Key Indicators Report. Values in parentheses (e.g. Ekiti) indicate estimates based on 25–49 unweighted cases and should be interpreted with caution.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 3 — Inspect the data
Before building any chart, always look at your data first.

# View the first few rows
head(coverage)

      state penta3_coverage
1      Abia            79.7
2   Adamawa            59.2
3 Akwa Ibom            72.8
4   Anambra            78.6
5    Bauchi            58.2
6   Bayelsa            73.4

# Check dimensions — how many rows and columns?
nrow(coverage)  # should be 37 (36 states + FCT)

[1] 37

ncol(coverage)  # should be 2

[1] 2

# Quick summary of coverage values
summary(coverage$penta3_coverage)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.90   47.30   62.20   59.99   75.90   94.60 


summary() gives you the minimum, maximum, and average coverage values at a glance, useful for understanding the spread before you visualise it.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 4 — Build the “before” chart
This is the chart most analysts would produce — technically correct, but built for the analyst, not the decision maker.

# The "before" chart — a label, not an argument
chart_before <- ggplot(
  data = coverage,
  aes(
    x = reorder(state, penta3_coverage),  # order states from lowest to highest
    y = penta3_coverage                    # coverage on the y axis
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#AAAAAA") +            # draw bars in grey
  coord_flip() +                           # flip so state names are readable
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),     # format y axis as percentages
    limits = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Penta3 Coverage by State, Nigeria 2023-24",  # a label
    x = NULL,
    y = "Coverage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# View the chart
chart_before








Notice the title: “Penta3 Coverage by State, Nigeria 2023–24.”
It tells you what the chart is. It does not tell you what to do about it.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
section: Step 5 — Find the argument in your data
text:
Step 5 — Find the argument in your data
Before building a better chart, we need to identify the decision hiding in the data.

# Calculate the national average
national_avg <- mean(coverage$penta3_coverage)
national_avg  # print the value

[1] 59.99459

# How many states are below the national average?
coverage %>%
  filter(penta3_coverage < national_avg) %>%
  arrange(penta3_coverage)

     state penta3_coverage
1   Sokoto            10.9
2  Zamfara            12.6
3    Kebbi            13.1
4    Kwara            34.9
5    Niger            36.7
6     Kogi            37.1
7    Borno            42.2
8    Benue            44.3
9  Plateau            47.1
10  Taraba            47.3
11    Kano            47.5
12  Kaduna            48.0
13    Yobe            51.3
14     Oyo            52.6
15 Katsina            53.3
16  Bauchi            58.2
17 Adamawa            59.2
18   Gombe            59.8


filter() keeps only rows where the condition is true — here, states where coverage falls below the national average. arrange() sorts them from lowest to highest so we can see the worst performers immediately.
This is your argument: a cluster of states — concentrated in the north — are significantly below the national average, and the gap between them and high-performing states is substantial.
That is a policy statement. Now let us build a chart that says it.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 6 — Build the “after” chart

# Flag each state as above or below the national average
coverage <- coverage %>%
  mutate(
    below_avg = penta3_coverage < national_avg  # creates a TRUE/FALSE column
  )

# The "after" chart — an argument, not a label
chart_after <- ggplot(
  data = coverage,
  aes(
    x = reorder(state, penta3_coverage),
    y = penta3_coverage,
    fill = below_avg                       # colour bars by above/below average
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = national_avg,             # reference line at national average
    linetype   = "dashed",
    colour     = "#333333",
    linewidth  = 0.6
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE"  = "#D85A30",                 # orange for below-average states
      "FALSE" = "#1D9E75"                  # green for above-average states
    ),
    guide = "none"                         # title explains colour — no legend needed
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom   = "text",
    x      = 3,
    y      = national_avg + 3,
    label  = paste0("National average: ", round(national_avg, 1), "%"),
    hjust  = 0,
    size   = 3,
    colour = "#333333"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "**Northern states are falling behind** — and the gap demands attention",
    subtitle = "Penta3 coverage by state, Nigeria 2023–24. <span style='color:#D85A30'>States below national average</span> highlighted in orange.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Coverage (%)",
    caption  = "Source: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2023–24 (PR157)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_markdown(size = 12, lineheight = 1.3),
    plot.subtitle = element_markdown(size = 10, colour = "#555555"),
    plot.caption  = element_text(size = 8, colour = "#999999")
  )

# View the chart
chart_after








Two things make this chart work differently from the first:

element_markdown() from ggtext lets us bold words in the title and colour text in the subtitle — so the reader’s eye goes exactly where we need it
The colour split between above and below average means the reader understands the argument before reading a single state name

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 7 — Compare before and after

# Place both charts side by side using patchwork
chart_before + chart_after +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Same data. Different decisions.",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
    )
  )








patchwork makes combining charts as simple as using +. plot_annotation() adds an overarching title across both panels.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
What just changed



Element
Before
After




Title
Describes the chart
Makes an argument


Colour
Uniform grey
Encodes meaning


Reference line
None
National average anchor


Annotation
None
Contextual label


Subtitle
None
Directs the reader’s eye



None of these changes require more analysis. They require a different question before you build the chart:
What do I need my reader to do with this?

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Your turn
Take a chart you have made recently. Look at the title. Ask yourself:

Does this title describe the chart, or does it make an argument?
What is the one thing I need my reader to decide after seeing this?
Can I rewrite the title to answer that question directly?
